newsitem.title: USA: IBM seen taking Dow lower at start.
newsitem.headline: IBM seen taking Dow lower at start.

text.p: Weakness in shares of International Business Machines Corp could take the Dow lower at the start of trade Thursday, following yesterday's 94 point drop, the third sharp selloff in four days.
IBM shares were off in London on a Wall Street Journal article saying that analysts were slimming down their earnings estimates for Big Blue in 1997.
Otherwise, analysts said, the market's correction appeared to be tailing off, with the biggest hurdle left for tomorrow -- the March employment report.

"IBM will be a negative for the Dow. Another crucial point is that the Nasdaq Composite closed at 1201 yesterday," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "If it goes below the 1200 level, it could bring selling into the high techs."

Cardillo said that he felt the market's correction was nearing an end. The blue chip average's declines over the last four sessions, including a modest gain on Tuesday, totaled almost 364 points, or 5.3 percent, the third largest point decline over any like period.
"I think we are at the tail end of the correction. The worst case scenario, if tomorrow's numbers show any substantial rise in wage costs, is 6350/6400 on the Dow," Cardillo said.

"The bond market is stabilizing. We had two days of a stable bond market and, yesterday, the stock market completely ignored it. That is because when a correction is drawing to an end, emotions override the fundamentals, which are still good."
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average gained 92.01 points, or 0.51 percent, to 18,129.31.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 6.7 at 4229.9.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, International Business Machines Corp shares were down two at 131-1/4.

Intel Corp slipped 1/2 to 136-1/2, while Texas Instruments eased 1/2 to 74-1/4. Apple Computer Inc bucked the trend, rising 1/4 to 18-1/4 after a report in the New York Times said the company was actively looking for a friendly merger partner.
Boeing Co dipped 3/8 to 98-1/8 in London after U.S. safety officials issued an emergency order to inspect the wing flap bolts on some of the aircraft makers 767 jets.
The dollar clung to around 123 yen in Tokyo and was just off its session lows in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly lower, with the long bond down 5/32 to yield 7.09 percent.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that some analysts are cutting their earnings estimates for IBM -- not just for the first and second quarters but for all of 1997.

The New York Times Market Place writes that 12 months after shares in Lucent Technologies Inc started trading in the largest initial public offering in Wall Street history, Lucent's stock is showing notable resilience in the midst of a broad technology selloff.
